entities.name: Petrus de Natalibus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Pietro Ungarello di Marco de' Natali, known to posterity as Petrus de Natalibus, served as the Bishop of Equilio (modern Jesolo) near Venice from 1370 until his death in 1406, establishing himself as a pivotal figure in late medieval hagiography. His monumental work, the *Catalogus Sanctorum* (Catalogue of Saints), compiled around 1372, became one of the most comprehensive and widely disseminated collections of saints' lives during the pre-Reformation era, providing a foundational resource for preachers, artists, and devotional readers across Catholic Europe and profoundly influencing the popular understanding of sanctity.

The *Catalogus Sanctorum* systematically documented the lives, miracles, and martyrdoms of approximately 1,500 saints, organized chronologically by their feast days throughout the liturgical year. Drawing upon a vast array of earlier hagiographical sources, including the *Legenda Aurea* of Jacobus de Voragine, various martyrologies, and local traditions, Natalibus meticulously synthesized these narratives. His critical contribution lay in the sheer scope and accessible structure of his compilation, which offered a practical and relatively standardized compendium for a diverse audience, from monastic communities seeking sermon material to lay individuals engaging in personal devotion.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Petrus de Natalibus's *Catalogus Sanctorum* became a foundational text for hagiography across Catholic Europe, influencing religious art and devotional practices for centuries. Its widespread dissemination, especially through early printing, solidified its role as a standard reference for understanding Christian saints.
